newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine peso falls into uncharted territory.
newsitem.headline: Philippine peso falls into uncharted territory.

text.p: The Philippine peso fell into new territory on Monday and could drop further with the central bank's decision to let it seek its own level, bankers and analysts said.

The peso, buffeted by the region's currency turmoil, hit a record low of 30.14 to the dollar in morning trade, or 14 percent below its level of 26.40 before the central bank's effective devaluation on July 11.

Volume was an active $70.5 million, although that is well below levels before the currency's slump last month when the central bank finally caved in to waves of speculative attacks on the currency that were eating up its reserves.
"It (the peso) will test further lows," a bank trader said.

"The central bank is not intervening at all. Probably for them, letting the exchange rate go is the lesser evil than controlling it through interest rates," said Emma Pante, economist at Far East Bank.

The central bank last month raised its closely watched overnight borrowing rate to a 2-1/2-year high of 32 percent in a futile defence of the peso which had fallen prey to attacks bedevilling Southeast Asia's currencies.
It has since brought down its overnight borrowing rate to 14 percent to encourage banks to lend and prevent a possible recession caused by high interest rates.
But the prolonged volatility in the region's currencies kept the peso on the defensive.

"By letting it (the peso) go, it will not go haywire for long. It will seek its own level," Pante said, adding the currency could trade at 30/30.5 before gaining again. "This week you'll see it appreciating."

"There's a common strategy among the central banks in the region to let their currencies seek their own level, which should bring us closer to stability earlier," an analyst from a foreign brokerage house said.

"They (the central bank) don't have much choice (in their intervention stance). They're already resigned to the fact there would be a lot more volatility before the peso seeks its own equilibrium level," said Banco Santander treasurer Antonio Agcaoili.
But he said the extent of the speculation in the market had been regulated by the central bank through new regulations set out last month.

These include the cutting of banks' long dollar positions to five percent from 10 percent of capital, the raising of liquidity reserves and the slashing of over-the-counter dollar sales limit to $25,000 from $100,000 per individual.
Bank traders said the central bank could still raise liquidity reserves to control the amount of liquidity that could be shifted to peso speculation.
"That's the central bank's prerogative. (But) that could be counter-productive to their goal of lowering of interest rates," Agcaoili said.
